topic.title: the third partner
topic.claim: In urban dual-income homes, the house help is the reason the marriage looks equal; her day off shows who really runs the house.

paragraphs: In most urban Indian homes, the marriage has a third partner.
She arrives at 8 and leaves by 11.
Both of you work. Both of you are tired. You split the rent, the EMI, the Netflix.
And the house runs so smoothly that nobody ever has to ask who does what.
Then one morning, the WhatsApp arrives.
"Didi, aaj nahi aaungi."
By 9 AM, the most honest audit of your marriage has begun.
Who does the dishes. Who sweeps. Who remembers the dusting nobody ever noticed she did.
And the audit usually reaches the same finding: the work doesn't split down the middle. It slides back to the wife.
India's own time-use survey says the same: women who do housework spend about five hours a day on it. Men, about an hour and a half.
Here's what nobody says out loud. Urban India never settled who does the housework.
It outsourced the question, for ₹10,000 a month, and called the answer equality.
That money buys back two, maybe three hours a day for the woman of the house.
It's probably the best-returning money the family spends. Nobody budgets it that way.
And the didi who sent that message has a home too.
Her own dishes, her own kids' tiffin, packed at 6 AM before she gets to yours. The equality you paid for ends at her doorstep.
So when that message comes, don't treat it as a crisis. Treat it as a mirror.
One day a month, it shows you who actually runs your house.
She isn't the help.
She's the reason your marriage looks equal.

d53ae61263323bc707b39eabac9d67269cc9494b.broken_premise: Slides 5 and 7, and the third premise. The survey figures are real: in India's Time Use Survey 2024, women who do any unpaid domestic work average about 289 minutes a day (about 4.8 hours), and men who do it average 88 minutes. But these are national averages across all households, rural and urban, and most of those households pay no domestic worker. The survey does not split results by whether a household has paid help. So it cannot show that women spend this time 'whatever help they have', or that 'the five hours the survey counts are what's left' after the didi's work. The ~5 hours is the total for a typical woman, not what remains in a dual-income urban home with a maid. Summaries also report urban women's figure as a bit lower (around 232–241 minutes vs ~5 hours), though the secondary sources disagree with each other. The post uses the national number to stand in for its target household, and that is wrong.
d53ae61263323bc707b39eabac9d67269cc9494b.actual_mechanism: The Time Use Survey records a day of activity for each person aged 6 and over. 'Minutes per participant' means the average among people who did any of that activity that day. Paid domestic work done by a hired worker counts in her own time use, not in the employer household's, and the survey does not group employer households by whether they hire help. The data supports a large and persistent gender gap in unpaid housework, nationally and in urban areas. It does not measure how much housework is left for the wife after a maid's shift.
